refuse_supplier_choice.question: Which electricity supplier should I switch to for the cheapest tariff?

If you have a question on any of those, such as wind generation or day-ahead prices for a given period, I can help with that.

installed_solar_vs_2030_target.question: How much solar capacity is installed in Germany, and what is the 2030 target?

input.b_label: installed solar AC, end of October 2026 (GW)

content.text:
Germany had about 120.7 GW of solar capacity installed at the end of October 2026 (AC/inverter basis; the November 2026 figure so far is 121.0 GW). On the module (DC) basis it was about 132.7 GW. The EEG 2023 target is 215 GW by 2030, which is 94.3 GW (ratio 1.78) above the October 2026 AC figure. negative_price_hours_october.question: For how many hours were day-ahead electricity prices negative in October 2026?

That is 7 quarter-hour intervals out of 2,980 (745 hours) covered, with no missing data. Negative prices were not counted at exactly zero, since the threshold was strictly below 0 EUR/MWh.

hours_above_300_october.question: How many hours in October 2026 had a day-ahead price above 300 EUR/MWh?

content.text:

Counting the 15-minute values directly gives 110 intervals, or 27.5 hours. The gap is because short price spikes can average out below 300 EUR/MWh within an hour.

Period: 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-31 (German local time). Price data had no gaps.

Source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE), day-ahead prices, CC BY 4.0. Calculation: own, on these prices.

solar_market_value_october.question: What was the market value (capture price) of solar power in October 2026, and how does it compare with the official value?

input.a_label: Own solar capture price, Oct 2026 (Energy-Charts generation, 15-min)

content.text:
In October 2026 (1–31 Oct, German local time), the solar capture price in Germany was **13.45 ct/kWh (134.49 EUR/MWh)**, calculated from Energy-Charts solar generation and day-ahead prices. The official solar market value for the same month is **13.39 ct/kWh**, so the difference is +0.06 ct/kWh (+0.44 %). The official figure is reported, not final, and it comes from the TSOs' feed-in extrapolation, so small differences are expected. Our solar capture rate was 79.45 % of the average spot price of 16.93 ct/kWh, which matches the official spot average.

Source: Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE) for solar generation; Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info for day-ahead prices; official market value from netztransparenz.de (German TSOs), as reported by Solarserver (published 2026-11-10, status: reported).

It covers direct emissions from German generation divided by electricity consumed in Germany, and excludes emissions abroad from net imports.

Source: Umweltbundesamt (UBA), Climate Change 16/2026 (published 2026-03-23)

price_week_vs_october.question: How did the average day-ahead price last week compare with the October 2026 average?

content.text:
Last week's average day-ahead price was 256.59 EUR/MWh (25.659 ct/kWh), which is 87.32 EUR/MWh or 51.6 % above the October 2026 average of 169.27 EUR/MWh (16.927 ct/kWh). Last week is Monday 2–Sunday 8 November 2026, and the averages are simple means of the 15-minute prices over each period.

Source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE)

followup_wind_solar_ratio.question: So how many times bigger was wind's share than solar's?

content.text:
Wind supplied **23.3%** of Germany's public net generation from Monday 2 to Sunday 8 November 2026 (2,098.68 GWh of 9,007.51 GWh total). Wind includes onshore and offshore. This uses Energy-Charts' public net generation basis; including industrial self-supply would give a different share, which I did not calculate.

Source: Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE)

Solar supplied **7.75%** of Germany's public net generation from Monday 2 to Sunday 8 November 2026 (697.67 GWh of 9,007.51 GWh total). For comparison, wind was 23.3% in the same week.

Source: Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE)

Wind's share was about **3.0 times** solar's in Monday 2 to Sunday 8 November 2026 (23.3% vs. 7.75% of public net generation; ratio 3.006). The gap is 15.55 percentage points.

Source: Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE)

wind_speed_last_week.question: How windy was it in Germany last week?

content.text:
Last week (Monday 2 to Sunday 8 November 2026) was calm to light-breezy in Germany. The average station wind speed across the 65 DWD stations was 3.34 m/s, with a peak hourly mean of 5.64 m/s on 4 November at 13:00. The windiest day was 4 November (4.78 m/s mean) and the calmest was 8 November (2.31 m/s).

This is an indicator measured about 10 m above ground, not the wind at turbine hub height, so it does not show what turbines actually received.

Source: Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD), 65 stations, CC BY 4.0

price_calm_vs_windy_october.question: In October 2026, how did the day-ahead price in hours with little wind compare with windy hours?

input.a_label: Day-ahead price, hours with wind below 3 m/s, Oct 2026
input.b_label: Day-ahead price, hours with wind above 5 m/s, Oct 2026

content.text:
In October 2026 (1–31 Oct, German local time), the day-ahead price averaged 214.84 EUR/MWh in hours with little wind (station wind below 3 m/s, 304 hours) and 62.61 EUR/MWh in windy hours (above 5 m/s, 144 hours). The difference is 152.23 EUR/MWh, a ratio of 3.43. The all-hours average was 169.27 EUR/MWh.

Wind is the DWD station mean at about 10 m height over 65 stations, so it is an indicator of how windy it was, not what turbines received. The thresholds (3 and 5 m/s) are my choice, not official definitions. These are associations: demand, gas prices and imports also affect prices. Hourly weather was matched to hourly price averages (745 hours).

Source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info (day-ahead prices, CC BY 4.0); Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD), opendata.dwd.de (wind, CC BY 4.0).

dunkelflaute_hours_october.question: How many hours in October 2026 had neither wind nor sun?

content.text:
**209 hours** in October 2026 (1–31 October, German local time) had neither wind nor sun, about 28 % of the 745 hours covered. I used wind speed below 3 m/s and solar radiation below 50 W/m², both my assumptions rather than official definitions. Wind is the station mean at about 10 m height over 65 DWD stations, so it is an indicator of how windy it was, not what turbines received.

Source: Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD), CC BY 4.0, via opendata.dwd.de

followup_gas_in_dunkelflaute.question: How much power did gas plants produce on average in those hours?

content.text:
**209 hours** in October 2026 (1–31 October, German local time) had both wind speed below 3 m/s and solar radiation below 50 W/m². That is 28.05% of the 745 hours with data.

These thresholds are my assumptions, not official definitions. Wind is the DWD station mean at about 10 m above ground across 65 stations, so it indicates how windy it was rather than what turbines received. The count is of hourly means.

Source: Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD), CC BY 4.0, opendata.dwd.de

input.a_label: gas, mean in the 209 low-wind, no-sun hours, Oct 2026
input.b_label: gas, mean over all hours, Oct 2026

content.text:
In the 209 hours of October 2026 with wind below 3 m/s and solar radiation below 50 W/m², gas plants produced 9,310 MW on average (public net generation). Across all 745 hours of October, the average was 6,816 MW, so the low-wind, no-sun hours were 2,494 MW (36.6%) higher.

Thresholds are my assumptions: wind is the DWD station mean at about 10 m height, an indicator rather than turbine hub-height wind. The gas figure is an hourly average of 15-minute values, and the link to gas output is an association, not proof of cause (demand and imports also matter).

Source: Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE) for generation; Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD), CC BY 4.0, opendata.dwd.de for weather.

weather_today_not_available.question: How windy is it in Germany today?

content.text:
I can't tell you how windy it is today (14 Nov 2026): the DWD weather data only runs up to yesterday. For yesterday, Friday 13 Nov 2026, the mean wind speed across 65 DWD stations was 4.6 m/s, with a peak hourly mean of 5.3 m/s at 12:00. The station wind is measured about 10 m above ground, so it indicates how windy it was rather than what turbine hubs received.

price_germany_vs_france_last_week.question: Was electricity cheaper in France or in Germany last week?

content.text:
France was marginally cheaper on average last week, but the gap was very small.

- **Averages, Monday 2 to Sunday 8 November 2026 (day-ahead, 15-minute values):** Germany 256.59 EUR/MWh (25.659 ct/kWh) and France 255.83 EUR/MWh (25.583 ct/kWh). Germany was 0.76 EUR/MWh (0.3 %) higher.
- **Hours:** Germany was cheaper than France in 87 hours, dearer in 39.5 hours and equal in 41.5 hours, so France was more often the cheaper zone.

Source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE). Prices are day-ahead values; the hour counts are from 15-minute intervals and may differ slightly from hourly averages.

hours_france_cheaper_last_week.question: In how many hours last week was power cheaper in France than in Germany?

content.text:
In the week of 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-08 (Monday to Sunday, German local time), French day-ahead prices were below German ones in **39.5 hours** (158 of 672 quarter-hours). Germany was cheaper in 87.0 hours, and prices were equal in 41.5 hours.

I counted quarter-hours with a positive spread (Germany minus France) and divided by four. The hour totals are from 15-minute values, so they may differ slightly from an hourly-average count.

Source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE), CC BY 4.0

followup_commercial_imports_from_france.question: How much did Germany import from France in those hours, according to the scheduled commercial exchanges?

content.text:
In the week of 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-08 (Mon–Sun, German time), France's day-ahead price was lower than Germany's in **47 hours** (28% of 168 hours) when hourly averages are used. On a 15-minute basis the count is 39.5 hours. The gap comes from how the two methods count, not from different data. Hours with equal prices are excluded from both counts.

Source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE), day-ahead prices for DE-LU and FR, own calculation.

In the 47 hours of 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-08 when France's day-ahead price was lower than Germany's (hourly-average basis), Germany's scheduled commercial exchanges with France were a **net import of 91.22 GWh**. That is positive, so Germany imported from France on net in those hours.

Source: Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE), scheduled commercial exchanges; Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info, day-ahead prices; own calculation.

renewable_curtailment_last_week.question: How much renewable generation was curtailed by redispatch last week?

content.text:
Renewable generation curtailed by redispatch in Germany was 1,724 MWh (1.72 GWh) from Monday 2 to Sunday 8 November 2026. That is about 1.7 GWh of the 2,884 MWh total redispatch reductions in the same week, and the rest was conventional plants. The three TSOs' shares of reductions were TenneT DE 1,604 MWh, Amprion 920 MWh and 50Hertz 360 MWh. The figures exclude one plant test run and include one countertrading measure. Each measure's energy is spread evenly over its window, so any hourly breakdown is approximate.

Source: netztransparenz.de (German TSOs)

redispatch_by_operator_last_week.question: Which transmission system operator ordered the most redispatch reductions last week?

content.text:
**TenneT DE** ordered the most redispatch reductions in the week of 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-08 (Monday to Sunday): 1,604 MWh. Amprion ordered 920 MWh and 50Hertz 360 MWh; TransnetBW ordered none. These are the energy totals for each measure within the period, excluding one plant test run and one countertrading measure.

Source: netztransparenz.de (German TSOs)

curtailment_in_windy_hours.question: How much of last week's renewable curtailment happened in hours with wind above 4 m/s?

input.a_label: renewable curtailment in hours with wind above 4 m/s, 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-08

content.text:
About 1,204 MWh of last week's renewable curtailment (≈70 % of the week's 1,724 MWh) happened in hours with station wind above 4 m/s. That covered 43 of 168 hours (25.6 %).

Period: Monday 2026-11-02 to Sunday 2026-11-08 (German local time). Wind is the DWD mean over 65 stations at about 10 m height, so it is an indicator of how windy it was, not the wind at turbine hub height. The curtailment series spreads each measure's energy evenly over its window, so the hourly split is approximate. The 4 m/s threshold is my choice.

Source: netztransparenz.de (German TSOs) for redispatch; Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD) for wind speed.

battery_last_week.question: How much could a 10 MW / 20 MWh battery have earned on the German day-ahead market last week?

content.text:
A 10 MW / 20 MWh battery would have earned about **€18,164** on the German day-ahead market from Monday 2 to Sunday 8 November 2026, or about €1,816 per MW over the week (roughly €2,595 per day).

- **Assumptions:** 90% round-trip efficiency, no wear cost, starting and ending each day empty.
- **Operation:** 271 MWh charged and 244 MWh discharged, about 12.9 full cycles (1.8 per day).
- **Prices:** average buy price €217.09/MWh and average sell price €315.56/MWh.
- **Best and worst days:** 5 November (€3,762) and 7 November (€1,495).

This is an upper bound from my own calculation on day-ahead prices. It ignores intraday and balancing markets, grid fees, taxes and bidding risk.

Source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE), day-ahead prices for DE-LU; battery result is an own calculation.

battery_october_default_size.question: What could a battery have earned on the German day-ahead market in October 2026?

content.text:
A 1 MW / 2 MWh battery would have earned about **EUR 11,000 (≈ EUR 11,001 per MW) on the German day-ahead market in October 2026** (1–31 Oct), or about EUR 355 per day. That is an upper bound from my own calculation on day-ahead prices. It assumes perfect foresight of each day's prices, a 90 % round-trip efficiency, zero wear cost, and no grid fees, taxes, intraday or balancing revenue.

- Revenue: EUR 29,131; charging cost: EUR 18,131
- Energy charged: 149.4 MWh; discharged: 134.5 MWh; losses: 14.9 MWh
- Full cycles: 70.9 in the month (about 2.3 per day)
- Average buy price: EUR 121.34/MWh; average sell price: EUR 216.63/MWh
- Best day: 29 Oct 2026 (EUR 677); worst day: 23 Oct 2026 (EUR 106)

Source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE), day-ahead prices for DE-LU; battery result is own calculation.

flexible_load_yesterday.question: An electrolyser can use 20 MWh at up to 5 MW. When would that have been cheapest yesterday, and how much would it have saved compared with running evenly through the day?

content.text:
On 2026-11-13 (Berlin time), the 20 MWh would have been cheapest in one block at 5 MW from 10:30 to 14:30, running 4 hours. The average price paid was 97.09 EUR/MWh (cost 1,941.84 EUR). Running evenly over the day would have averaged 161.73 EUR/MWh (3,234.70 EUR), so the saving was 1,292.86 EUR (39.97%). This uses day-ahead prices only, without grid fees, taxes or levies.

Source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de via Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE), day-ahead price for DE-LU; own calculation.

register_wind_nrw_since_2023.question: How much onshore wind capacity was added in North Rhine-Westphalia since 2023, and how much is installed now?

content.text:
Between 2023 and 2026, 3,530.85 MW of onshore wind (726 units) was added in North Rhine-Westphalia. About 395.1 MW (366 units) was permanently decommissioned in the same period, so the net change is 3,135.75 MW. Installed onshore wind capacity is 9,899.26 MW (4,063 units) as of the register date 2026-10-01, the latest available. Years are commissioning years, and 2026 figures are preliminary because units are often registered late. A further 13,144.03 MW is registered as planned (not yet built).

Source: Marktstammdatenregister (Bundesnetzagentur), dl-de/by-2-0, register date 2026-10-01

register_lignite_top_district_nrw.question: Which district in NRW has the most lignite power plant capacity?

content.text:
The Rhein-Erft-Kreis has the most lignite capacity in NRW: 2,471.8 MW across 9 units, or 41.69% of the state's 5,928.3 MW. The Rhein-Kreis Neuss (2,120.0 MW) and the Städteregion Aachen (1,319.0 MW) follow. Installed capacity is as of the register date 2026-10-01, and no lignite units were added or decommissioned in 2026 so far.

Source: Marktstammdatenregister (Bundesnetzagentur), dl-de/by-2-0, register date 2026-10-01
